title: Truck meets car: who pushes harder?
hook: A truck ten times heavier hits a car head-on. Does it push harder than it gets pushed?

knows: heavy trucks wreck small cars in crashes
a push or pull is a force
doesNotKnow: that acceleration, not force, is what differs

misconception: The bigger object hits harder, so it exerts a bigger force on the smaller one than the smaller exerts back.
objective: The learner can explain that in a collision the two objects push on each other equally hard at every instant, and that the lighter one changes velocity more because a = F / m.

claims.text: When two objects push on each other, each feels a force of the same size in the opposite direction, at every instant (Newton's third law).
claims.source: Newton, Principia (1687), Law III; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5 (Newton's third law).

claims.text: The same force changes the 1,000 kg car's velocity ten times as much as the 10,000 kg truck's.
claims.source: a = F / m for each vehicle with the same F, so a_car / a_truck = 10,000 / 1,000 = 10; integrated over the contact, delta v_car / delta v_truck = 10. Simulation: truck 10 -> 7.59 m/s (change 2.41), car -10 -> +14.09 m/s (change 24.09), ratio 10.00.

claims.text: In the crash shown (both at 10 m/s, 10,000 kg truck), by the end the car's speed has changed by about 24.1 m/s (its velocity reverses) and the truck's by about 2.4 m/s.
claims.source: 1D head-on collision, truck +10 m/s, car -10 m/s; contact modelled as a spring-damper F = max(0, k d + c d'), k = 5e5 N/m, damping for restitution about 0.2; RK4 at 1e-5 s. Momentum conserved: 10,000 x 7.59 + 1,000 x 14.09 = 90,000 kg m/s = 10,000 x 10 - 1,000 x 10. | v2 (2026-10-14): reveal quotes speed changes read from the stage, gated on playing the crash to its end; previous verification void, needs re-check. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: VERIFIED for the 10,000 kg truck (own semi-implicit Euler at 1e-6 s: 24.09 and 2.41 m/s; car -10 to +14.09). Note: the reveal quotes end-of-run values for whatever truck mass is set, so the numbers are right for each mass but only the 10,000 kg case is recorded here.

claims.text: The force sizes shown (peaks of roughly 300 to 400 kN over about 0.1 s) come from an illustrative contact model, not a measured crash; the equality of the two forces does not depend on the model.
claims.source: Same simulation as c3: peak 293 kN (1,000 kg truck), 395 kN (10,000 kg), 404 kN (20,000 kg); contact lasts 77 to 107 ms. The model applies one contact force to both bodies, so equality is Newton's third law by construction.

claims.text: The car comes off worse because its speed changes far more, not because it is pushed harder.
claims.source: Injury risk scales with the acceleration experienced by occupants; with equal forces, a = F / m is ten times larger for the car (c1, c2). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 9 (collisions and impulse). | v2 (2026-10-14): reveal quotes speed changes read from the stage, gated on playing the crash to its end; previous verification void, needs re-check. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: DISPUTED as staged. The reveal quotes the speed changes for the current truck-mass slider (1,000 to 20,000 kg) and always says "the same push changes the lighter vehicle much more. That is why the car comes off worse." At 1,000 kg (slider minimum) both change by 13.25 m/s (own sim), so the reveal contradicts its own numbers; at 2,000 kg the ratio is only 2. Fix (builder): pin the reveal figures to the 10,000 kg crash, or word it by mass ratio and drop "much more" when masses are close, or set the slider minimum above 1,000 kg. The physics in the claim text holds for the 10,000 kg truck.

claims.text: 1 kN (a thousand newtons) is about the weight of a 100 kg person.

recall.question: A mosquito splats on a moving bus windscreen. During the impact, how does the force of the bus on the mosquito compare with the force of the mosquito on the bus?
recall.why: Forces come in equal and opposite pairs; the mosquito suffers because the same force gives its tiny mass a huge acceleration.
